pages.name: The guess
pages.text: The spring obeys `m x″ + c x′ + k x = 0`. Try the guess that solved decay, `x = e^(rt)`. Each derivative brings out one `r`. Then every term carries `e^(rt)`. That factor is never zero, so it drops out. What is left is `m r² + c r + k = 0`. This is the [[characteristic equation]]. Its two roots are rates, per second. They decide how the mass moves.

pages.name: Find the roots
pages.task: At damping 5, the characteristic equation is `r² + 5r + 4 = 0`. What are its two roots?
pages.why: It factorises as `(r + 1)(r + 4) = 0`. So `r` = −1 or `r` = −4. Check one: 1 − 5 + 4 = 0. The roots multiply to 4 and add to −5. In general they multiply to `k ÷ m` and add to `−c ÷ m`.

pages.name: The roots and the motion
pages.text: The roots are `r = (−c ± √(c² − 4mk)) ÷ 2m`. The sign of `c² − 4mk` sorts three kinds of motion. The dots on the left are the roots. As the damping falls from 6 to 4, the roots slide together along the real axis, and the mass creeps back. At 4 they meet at −2. Below 4 they split into a mirror pair, and the trace rings. At 0 they sit on the j axis, at ±j2. Then, in this ideal model, the ringing never dies.

pages.name: Where they meet
pages.task: Which damping makes the two roots meet?
pages.why: They meet when `c² − 4mk` is zero, so the square root adds nothing. Then `c² = 4mk`. Here `4mk` = 4 × 1 × 4 = 16. So `c` = √16 = 4 N·s/m. That is `2√(mk)`, the critical damping.

pages.name: Two decays
pages.text: At damping 5, the roots are −1 and −4. Each real root gives a decay, and the answer adds the two, `x = A e^(−t) + B e^(−4t)`. Starting at 0.5 m gives `A + B = 0.5`. Starting at rest gives `−A − 4B = 0`. So `A` = 0.667 and `B` = −0.167. Each part is drawn faintly. The fast part has almost gone by 1 s. So the slow root sets the creep. This is [[overdamped]].
pages.alt: c equals 5 newton seconds per metre. The slow part and the fast part add to the creep. By 1 second the fast part has almost gone. minus 1. minus 4. 1 s.

pages.name: Heavier damping
pages.task: Now the damping is 6, and the roots are −0.76 and −5.24. Does the mass get back faster or slower than at damping 5?
pages.answer: Slower, because the slow root is nearer zero
pages.why: The roots always multiply to `k ÷ m` = 4 and add to `−c ÷ m`. At damping 6 they add to −6, not −5. To keep the product at 4, the fast root moves away from zero and the slow one moves in. The slow root sets the creep, and a root of −0.76 dies slower than −1. At 2 s the mass is still 0.13 m out, against 0.09 m at damping 5.
pages.alt: c equals 6 newton seconds per metre. the slow root moved in, from minus 1 to minus 0.76. at 2 s: 0.13 m out, against 0.09 m. The rings mark the roots at damping 5, the dots the roots at damping 6. minus 0.76. minus 5.24. 2 s.
options: Slower, because the slow root is nearer zero
Faster, because more damping stops it sooner
The same, because the start is the same

pages.name: Critical
pages.text: [[Critical damping]] is the quickest return that never swings past rest. At damping 4, the roots meet at −2, one root twice. So the answer needs a second part, `x = (0.5 + t)e^(−2t)`. Then `x′ = −2t e^(−2t)` and `x″ = (4t − 2)e^(−2t)`. Put in, `x″ + 4x′ + 4x` = 0. At 2 s it is 0.05 m out, nearer than with damping 5. Damping 3 reaches rest sooner, at about 1.8 s, but swings past it.
pages.alt: c equals 4 newton seconds per metre. At damping 4 the mass returns fastest without swinging past rest. At damping 3 it crosses rest and swings a little past. minus 2, twice. 0.05 m. swings past rest.

pages.name: One root, twice
pages.task: At damping 4, why can't `A e^(−2t)` alone be the answer?
pages.answer: It has one constant, and the start needs two values
pages.why: The start fixes two values, the position and the speed. One constant can match only one of them. With `A` = 0.5 the position fits, but the mass would start moving instead of at rest. So a second part, `t e^(−2t)`, brings a second constant.

pages.name: Ringing
pages.text: At damping 2, the roots are a mirror pair `α ± jβ`, here −1 ± j1.732. The trace rings inside a ghost [[envelope]], `e^(αt)`. The real part, −1, sets how fast it dies. The j part, 1.732, sets how fast it rings, in radians a second. With the switch on, an arrow shrinks as it turns. Its shadow on the real axis is the trace. The mirror root's arrow turns the other way, so the two add to a real number. The mass moves only up and down. This is [[underdamped]].

pages.name: Read the pair
pages.task: What do the roots −1 ± j1.732 say?
pages.answer: The envelope falls to 0.368 of itself each second, and it rings at 1.732 rad/s
pages.why: The real part, −1, sets the envelope `e^(−t)`. Each second it keeps `e^(−1)` = 0.368 of itself. The j part, 1.732, is how fast it rings, in radians a second. It would ring for ever only if the real part were 0.
pages.alt: c equals 2 newton seconds per metre. e to the power minus 1 equals 0.368 kept each second. it rings at 1.732 radians a second. At damping 2 the roots are a mirror pair, minus 1 plus or minus j1.732. The trace rings while its swings die. minus 1 plus j1.732. minus 1 minus j1.732. dies. rings. times 0.368 each second.
options: The envelope falls to 0.368 of itself each second, and it rings at 1.732 rad/s
The envelope falls to 0.368 each second, and it rings at 1 rad/s
It rings at 1.732 rad/s and never dies

pages.name: Two sketches
pages.task: Two sketches start from 0.5 m. In A, the peaks halve each swing. In B, they drop 0.1 m each swing. Which could come from `m x″ + c x′ + k x = 0`?
pages.why: In this equation the drag grows in step with the speed. So each swing keeps the same fraction of the last, as `e^(αt)` does. In A that fraction is always 0.5. In B it is 0.8, then 0.75. A ship's roll at small angles dies away like A, and its damping grows with forward speed. A drag of fixed size, such as dry friction, is not in this equation.
pages.alt: A: 0.25 divided by 0.5 equals 0.5, and 0.125 divided by 0.25 equals 0.5. B: 0.4 divided by 0.5 equals 0.8, but 0.3 divided by 0.4 equals 0.75. Sketch A has peaks 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 metres. Sketch B has peaks 0.5, 0.4, 0.3 metres. 0.5 m. 0.25 m. 0.125 m. 0.5 m. 0.4 m. 0.3 m.

pages.name: The loop
pages.task: A 100 mH coil, a 10 µF capacitor and 40 Ω sit in one loop. What does it do?
pages.answer: It rings near 980 rad/s inside an `e^(−200t)` envelope
pages.why: In base units, `L` = 0.1 H and `1 ÷ C` = 100000. Then `R²` = 1600 is smaller than `4L ÷ C` = 40000, so it rings. The roots are (−40 ± √(1600 − 40000)) ÷ 0.2. That is −200 ± j980, near enough. So it rings at about 980 rad/s, which is 156 Hz, inside an envelope `e^(−200t)`. That is just below the 1000 rad/s, or 159 Hz, this pair resonates at.
